title: NHRC, India takessuo motucognizance of reported death of 19 CRPF personnel between January to May 2026, as per the official data compiled by CRPF
subtitle:
Reportedly, the CRPF recorded the highest 59 suicides by its personnel in 2025
The Commission issues notices to the Home Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs and the CRPF Director General, calling for a detailed report on the matter within two weeks
body_text:
The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), India has taken suo motu cognizance of a media report that 19 Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) personnel died by suicide in less than five months between January and 22nd May 2026. According to the reported CRPF data, the force lost 59 personnel due to suicide in 2025. Reportedly, this was the highest number of suicides recorded in the last five years.
The Commission has observed that the contents of the news report, if true, raise serious issues of violation of the right to life of the personnel working with the largest Central Armed Police Force of the country. Therefore, it has issued notices to the Home Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs and the CRPF Director General, calling for a detailed report on the matter within two weeks.
According to the media report, carried on 11th August 2026, a total of 281 CRPF personnel died by suicide in the last five years. Of these, approximately 216 were on duty. The CRPF recorded 57 suicides in 2021, 43 in 2022, 57 in 2023, 46 in 2024 and 59 in 2025.
***
NSK

enrichment.summary: The NHRC has taken suo motu cognizance of media reports that 19 CRPF personnel died by suicide between January and 22 May 2026, following data showing the force recorded 59 suicides in 2025 — the highest in five years. It has issued notices to the Union Home Secretary and CRPF Director General seeking a detailed report within two weeks. Reports indicate 281 CRPF personnel died by suicide over the last five years (2021-2025), of which about 216 were on duty.
enrichment.context:
The CRPF, India's largest Central Armed Police Force (CAPF), has long faced concerns over the mental health and welfare of its personnel, who serve in high-stress environments including counter-insurgency, Naxal operations, and law-and-order duties, often with long separations from family and difficult postings. Rising suicide rates among CAPF personnel have periodically drawn parliamentary and judicial attention, prompting measures like stress-management programmes, buddy systems, regular home leave, yoga and counselling initiatives, and grievance redressal mechanisms. The NHRC's intervention here is significant because it frames these deaths as a potential violation of the right to life under Article 21, extending the right to life doctrine to the working conditions of security personnel rather than only civilians.

This is part of a broader pattern where the NHRC uses its suo motu powers under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 to seek accountability from state agencies without waiting for a formal complaint. Such interventions are recurring examinable events for governance and human rights sections of the UPSC syllabus, especially concerning institutional oversight mechanisms and the human rights of security forces.

prelims_questions.question: The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) derives its suo motu powers from which of the following?
options: The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993
The Armed Forces Special Powers Act, 1958
prelims_questions.explanation: The NHRC was established under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, which empowers it to take suo motu cognizance of human rights violations.

prelims_questions.question: Which of the following is the largest Central Armed Police Force (CAPF) in India?
prelims_questions.explanation: The CRPF is India's largest Central Armed Police Force, primarily responsible for internal security duties including counter-insurgency and law and order.

mains_questions.question: Discuss the factors contributing to rising suicide rates among personnel of Central Armed Police Forces in India. What institutional measures can be adopted to safeguard their mental health and right to life?

Examine the role of the National Human Rights Commission in ensuring accountability of state security agencies. Discuss the significance and limitations of its suo motu powers with reference to recent interventions.

mains.analytical_use: Helps analyse the evolving jurisprudence on Article 21 and the role of statutory bodies in enforcing accountability within security establishments.

mains.theme: Implementation gaps in CAPF welfare schemes
mains.analytical_use: Supports 'critically examine' questions on effectiveness of government welfare interventions for security forces.

mains.point: The episode illustrates the NHRC's institutional role in ensuring accountability of security agencies through suo motu notices rather than waiting for complaints.
mains.analytical_use: Useful for questions on the functioning and effectiveness of NHRC as an oversight body vis-à-vis executive agencies.

mains.theme: Operational stress in internal security duties
